ocar.opportunity: Local cortical circuits contain thousands of neurons and millions of synapses, so relating in-vivo activity to the underlying excitatory wiring is a route to the organizational logic of those networks.
ocar.challenge: For layer 2/3 pyramidal cells in mouse V1, physiology suggested that similarly tuned neurons excite each other, but the anatomical basis of that recurrent network was unknown.
ocar.action: Lee, Bonin, Reid and colleagues combined in-vivo calcium imaging with large-scale transmission electron microscopy (TEMCA), then traced axons, dendrites, and synapses in an aligned volume of superficial mouse visual cortex.
ocar.resolution: Among 1,278 reconstructed neuronal targets, a 201-neuron core (degree ≥ 2) was modular (Qmean = 0.55 ± 0.003 vs 0.50 ± 0.009 in permutations). Forty-three functionally characterized neurons made 990 synapses (443 onto inhibitory cells, 547 onto pyramidal cells). Similarly orientation-selective pyramids preferentially synapsed with each other, and those synapses were larger, even though axons and dendrites of all selectivities passed within <5 μm with roughly equal probability.
ocar.future_work: The authors predict that the mechanisms of functionally specific connectivity act at the length scale of spines, and they released the aligned EM volume at neurodata.io/lee16 for further analysis.

summaries.beginner: In mouse visual cortex, nerve cells that like the same line orientation tend to talk to each other. This team imaged those cells while they were alive, then used electron microscopy to show that the preference is built into the wiring, not just into which axons happen to pass nearby.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2016), Lee, Bonin, Reid and colleagues combined two-photon calcium imaging with large-scale EM of mouse V1 layer 2/3. A reconstructed excitatory network was modular, and 43 visually characterized neurons made 990 synapses, with a large fraction onto inhibitory cells. Pyramidal pairs with similar orientation preference were more likely to connect (Cochran–Armitage P < 0.05), and similarly tuned pairs formed larger synapses, despite potential contacts (<5 μm axon–dendrite proximity) being roughly equal across orientations. The authors argue that specificity is implemented at spines rather than by axonal geometry.
summaries.advanced: The functional analysis is restricted to cells with reproducible visual responses and excludes stimulus-edge effects; most of the 1,278 reconstructed targets were not physiologically characterized. Preferential excitatory connectivity is reported as statistically significant but not as a complete wiring rule, and the large inhibitory synapse fraction is discussed as a possible L2/3 mouse-V1 characteristic. Potential-synapse geometry is used to argue against a purely geometric explanation, but spine-level mechanisms are a prediction rather than a demonstrated molecular process. The selected PDF is an author manuscript of the Nature paper.

plain_language_summary: In mouse visual cortex, nerve cells that like the same line orientation tend to talk to each other. This team imaged those cells while they were alive, then used electron microscopy to show that the preference is built into the wiring, not just into which axons happen to pass nearby.

ocar.opportunity: As automated neuron segmentation improved, synapse annotation became a growing share of connectome reconstruction time—upwards of 50% of effort—so detecting synapses automatically is needed to keep reconstruction scaling.
ocar.challenge: Contact area is not a sufficient predictor of synaptic connection, Drosophila synapses are polyadic (one T-bar, many partners), and prior work had comparatively little automatic synapse detection relative to neuron tracing.
ocar.action: Huang, Scheffer, and Plaza detected presynaptic T-bars with a Deep and Wide Multiscale Recursive Network (DAWMR) and assigned postsynaptic partners with a multilayer perceptron whose features were conditioned on the local segmentation, then introduced metrics for connectomes of meaningful size.
ocar.resolution: On the Drosophila seven-column medulla dataset, automatic counts reconstructed high-multiplicity connections and preserved biological pathways, with only a small number of clear errors, outperforming a baseline that used body proximity as a synapse proxy.
ocar.future_work: Inference on volumes of several tera-voxels took on the order of weeks on up to two thousand cluster nodes, mostly in T-bar detection; the authors report ongoing work trading network width for depth in a convolutional T-bar detector to improve speed.

summaries.beginner: After computers learned to outline fly neurons in electron-microscope images, finding the actual synapses became the slow step. This paper automates that step for fruit-fly connections, where one sending site often talks to several partners at once.
summaries.intermediate: This 2016 study (Frontiers in Neural Circuits; selected PDF is the arXiv version) presents an end-to-end synapse detector for polyadic Drosophila synapses. Presynaptic T-bars are found with DAWMR; postsynaptic partners are assigned by an MLP using local segmentation features. Evaluated on the seven-column medulla connectome with new graph-level metrics, automatic predictions recovered high-multiplicity edges and biological pathways better than a contact-proximity baseline. Code is pointed to at github.com/janelia-flyem/flymatlib.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF is arXiv:1604.03075v1 and names DAWMR for T-bar detection; the catalog abstract for the later journal version mentions a U-Net CNN, so architecture details may have changed in the published Frontiers paper. Claims that most connectivity is characterized correctly are supported by custom metrics and log-scale edge-count plots, not by a single standard precision/recall number in the extracted text. Runtime on multi-teravoxel volumes remains a stated bottleneck. Evaluation is on Drosophila medulla, not vertebrate chemical synapses.

plain_language_summary: After computers learned to outline fly neurons in electron-microscope images, finding the actual synapses became the slow step. This paper automates that step for fruit-fly connections, where one sending site often talks to several partners at once.

ocar.opportunity: Serial electron microscopy can yield not only a wiring list but vesicle types, partner counts at boutons, and the spatial layout of inputs versus outputs on neuronal arbors.
ocar.challenge: Classic leech ultrastructure could describe neuropil cytology but not a functionally meaningful account of synaptic relationships, because sampling whole arbors was then impossible.
ocar.action: Pipkin, Bushong, Ellisman, and Kristan used serial block-face SEM to collect two volumes from medicinal-leech ganglia—an adult neuropil sample and an entire juvenile ganglion including somata—and reconstructed arbors with IMOD and TrakEM2.
ocar.resolution: Most arbors contained vesicle fields; some juvenile neurons (VE-4s) lacked vesicles or presynaptic varicosities in the ganglion, DE-3s almost entirely lacked them, DI-1s and VI-2s segregated vesicle-rich contralateral from vesicle-poor ipsilateral halves, and others (116s, S cell) mixed inputs and outputs throughout. No arbor or region was output-only.
ocar.future_work: The authors present these as the first large serial EM datasets from leech and as groundwork for future behavioral studies that link arbor polarity to function.

summaries.beginner: Leech nerve cells were long too tangled to map in full with electron microscopy. This team imaged adult and juvenile ganglia in 3D and found that some cells keep incoming and outgoing contacts in separate neighborhoods, while others mix them, and none were outgoing-only.
summaries.intermediate: In the Journal of Comparative Neurology (2016), Pipkin and colleagues collected two SBEM volumes from Hirudo verbana: a fraction of adult neuropil and an entire juvenile ganglion. They developed synapse criteria, scored vesicle types and apparent postsynaptic partners at boutons, and placed those findings on fully reconstructed juvenile arbors. Neurons segregated into input-only zones, mixed input/output zones, or input-only cells (e.g., VE-4s), with no purely presynaptic domains observed.
summaries.advanced: The adult volume samples only a small neuropil fraction, so mature-arbor completeness is limited; juvenile reconstructions supply whole ganglion-contained arbors but at a different developmental stage. Partner counts are “apparent” appositions by the authors’ criteria. No example of an output-only arbor region is reported, which is a negative finding in these volumes rather than a proof that such domains never occur. Behavioral linkage is explicitly future work.

plain_language_summary: Leech nerve cells were long too tangled to map in full with electron microscopy. This team imaged adult and juvenile ganglia in 3D and found that some cells keep incoming and outgoing contacts in separate neighborhoods, while others mix them, and none were outgoing-only.

ocar.opportunity: Only electron microscopy currently provides the resolution to reconstruct all synapses in a volume, and a whole-brain cellular connectome is argued to be needed to understand distributed neural computations.
ocar.challenge: Mesoscale atlases and diffusion MRI do not give complete connectivity of every neuron in one mammalian brain, and large-volume EM plus automated neurite reconstruction still face substantial obstacles.
ocar.action: Mikula reviews whole-brain sample preparation, ultramicrotomy, and high-throughput EM, and argues that the time is right to launch a concerted connectomic attack on a small mammalian whole brain.
ocar.resolution: The perspective holds that 10 nm in-plane resolution and 30 nm slice thickness can suffice for reliable circuit reconstructions in whole-mouse-brain preparations (citing Mikula and Denk 2015), while urging further validation across brain areas. A complete map is expected to test computational models and to revisit the “brain area” concept as a network of individual neurons rather than discrete parcels.
ocar.future_work: The piece calls for a small-mammal whole-brain effort; acknowledgments mention aldehyde-fixed Etruscan pygmy shrew brains as relevant material, but this article is not itself that reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: We still do not have a complete wiring diagram of any mammal’s brain. This perspective argues that sample preparation and electron microscopy have improved enough to try mapping a small mammalian brain end to end.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2016), Shawn Mikula reviews why mesoscale labeling atlases and MRI-based diffusion imaging cannot yield a cellular mammalian connectome, and why EM remains the resolution of record for synapses. He argues that whole-brain preparation and high-throughput EM now make a small-mammal whole-brain project timely, while large-volume acquisition and automated tracing remain bottlenecks. Cited parameters of 10 nm in-plane and 30 nm sections are presented as sufficient in mouse-brain preparations, pending broader validation.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a new whole-brain dataset or pipeline benchmark. Sufficiency of 10/30 nm sampling is attributed to prior work and flagged as needing validation in different areas. Super-resolution light microscopy is mentioned as a possible future alternative, not a current substitute. Claims about what a mammalian circuit diagram “will tell us” (brain-area revision, models of computation) are programmatic.

plain_language_summary: We still do not have a complete wiring diagram of any mammal’s brain. This perspective argues that sample preparation and electron microscopy have improved enough to try mapping a small mammalian brain end to end.

ocar.opportunity: Ascidian tadpole larvae are chordate in body plan with a tiny dorsal CNS, so a complete synaptic map can expose left–right brain asymmetry that is usually cryptic in larger brains.
ocar.challenge: Early neural development of Ciona was well studied, but detailed cellular organization of the swimming larva’s CNS had not been reported, and left–right pairing cannot be used to validate connections because many cells are not bilaterally paired.
ocar.action: Ryan, Lu, and Meinertzhagen reconstructed the synaptic connectome of one Ciona intestinalis tadpole larva from serial-section EM.
ocar.resolution: The larva’s 177 CNS neurons formed 6,618 synapses including 1,772 neuromuscular junctions, plus 1,206 gap junctions; 922 synapses were polyadic. Neurons are unipolar with at most a single dendrite; axo-axonal synapses predominate. Despite equal cell numbers on both sides, identities and pathways differ, including a right ocellus and left coronet cells.
ocar.future_work: The authors note that minor left/right differences might reflect developmental noise, because only a small number of larvae need survive, and they treat the map as a single-animal inventory of asymmetrical features rather than a population average.

summaries.beginner: A sea-squirt tadpole has a tiny chordate brain that is visibly lopsided. This paper maps every chemical and electrical connection among its 177 central neurons and shows that the two sides are not mirror images, even when cell counts match.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2016), Ryan, Lu, and Meinertzhagen report the CNS connectome of one Ciona intestinalis larva from serial-section EM: 177 neurons, 6,618 synapses (1,772 neuromuscular), 1,206 gap junctions, and 922 polyadic synapses. Cells are unipolar, often ciliated, and make few synapses, with axo-axonal contacts predominating. Sensory pathways into the motor ganglion are left–right asymmetric (coronet, antenna, and photoreceptor relays). Unlike some other connectomes, bilateral symmetry could not be used as a validation check.
summaries.advanced: This is a single larva; the authors explicitly cannot exclude developmental noise as a source of minor asymmetries. Some synapses are unpolarized or land on non-neuronal cells or basal lamina, complicating a simple directed graph. Pathway diagrams include weak connections drawn as dashed lines. Structural counterparts in vertebrates are suggested, not demonstrated by homology tests in this paper.

plain_language_summary: A sea-squirt tadpole has a tiny chordate brain that is visibly lopsided. This paper maps every chemical and electrical connection among its 177 central neurons and shows that the two sides are not mirror images, even when cell counts match.

ocar.opportunity: Glomerular olfactory systems are shared between insects and vertebrates, so a complete synaptic wiring diagram of a numerically simple antennal lobe can show how odor value and saliency are computed at the first synapse.
ocar.challenge: Even in adult Drosophila, only a few glomeruli had been partially reconstructed; the complete cell-type inventory and synaptic circuit of any glomerular olfactory system were unknown.
ocar.action: Berck, Khandelwal, Cardona and colleagues mapped the Drosophila larval antennal lobe with electron microscopy, including uniglomerular and multiglomerular projection neurons and local neurons, and released adjacency matrices of the full synaptic connectivity.
ocar.resolution: A canonical circuit of uniglomerular projection neurons relays gain-controlled olfactory receptor neuron activity to mushroom body and lateral horn. A parallel circuit of multiglomerular projection neurons and hierarchically connected local neurons integrates multiple receptor channels at the first synapse. Local-neuron to local-neuron synapses are proposed to implement bistable gain control: panglomerular inhibition for odor saliency, or allowing some glomeruli to report faint aversive odors against strong appetitive odors.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the diagram as a resource for experimental and theoretical work linking circuits to behavior, including the identified descending neuron reconstructed on both sides.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly larvae smell with a miniature version of the same glomerular layout used in our olfactory bulb. This preprint maps every connection in that first smell center and suggests two parallel paths: one that copies each odor channel onward, and another that mixes channels and can switch how strongly they compete.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2016), Berck, Khandelwal and colleagues reconstruct the complete Drosophila larval antennal lobe. Each glomerulus is defined by a single identified olfactory receptor neuron. Uniglomerular projection neurons feed mushroom body and lateral horn; multiglomerular projection neurons plus layered local neurons mix channels at the first synapse. LN–LN connectivity is interpreted as a putative bistable gain-control motif. Supplementary adjacency matrices give the full wiring.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF is a preprint (CC-BY-NC-ND), not the later journal version. The bistable gain-control mechanism is explicitly putative from anatomy. Completeness is claimed for this larval glomerular system; adult fly and vertebrate olfactory bulbs are analogized, not reconstructed here. Extracted text emphasizes circuit motifs more than synapse-count error rates.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly larvae smell with a miniature version of the same glomerular layout used in our olfactory bulb. This preprint maps every connection in that first smell center and suggests two parallel paths: one that copies each odor channel onward, and another that mixes channels and can switch how strongly they compete.

ocar.opportunity: Dense circuit reconstruction needs nanometer-scale 3D ultrastructure over fields of view that capture hundreds to thousands of packed neurons, which is a major driver of serial block-face SEM development.
ocar.challenge: Circuit mapping stresses volume EM on resolution, field of view, acquisition time, and sample preparation, while producing terabyte-scale datasets that need new processing workflows.
ocar.action: Wanner, Kirschmann, and Genoud review microtome-based SBEM for neuroscience, comparing it with serial-section TEM, ATUM-SEM, and FIB-SEM, and survey image-processing and analysis pipelines.
ocar.resolution: They summarize that SBEM and related volume-EM methods can resolve synapses and support dense reconstruction, that in-chamber diamond-knife milling is destructive unlike tape- or grid-collected sections, and that faster, larger acquisitions are flooding analysis software.
ocar.future_work: The review expects new protocols, microscopes, acquisition modes, and microtomes to keep expanding field of view and speed, with benefits beyond neuroscience.

summaries.beginner: To map every connection in a tangle of brain cells you need 3D electron microscopy, not ordinary light pictures. This review explains how a diamond knife inside a scanning electron microscope can shave and image a tissue block, and why the resulting data piles are so hard to analyze.
summaries.intermediate: In the Journal of Microscopy (2015), Wanner, Kirschmann, and Genoud review serial block-face SEM for circuit reconstruction. They contrast SBEM and FIB-SEM (destructive in-vacuum milling) with ssTEM and ATUM-SEM (section collection), note the need for <20 nm/pixel-scale ultrastructure, and discuss registration, tiling, and segmentation workflows for terabyte volumes. Connectomics is framed as a driver of SBEM hardware and software.
summaries.advanced: This is a short review (pp. 137–142), not a new reconstruction. It does not report original error rates or a single recommended pipeline. The cubic-millimeter MRI-voxel comparison (millions of neurons) is cited from other work to motivate scale, not measured here. Method choice tradeoffs are qualitative.

plain_language_summary: To map every connection in a tangle of brain cells you need 3D electron microscopy, not ordinary light pictures. This review explains how a diamond knife inside a scanning electron microscope can shave and image a tissue block, and why the resulting data piles are so hard to analyze.

ocar.opportunity: Automated segmentation is the bottleneck for dense connectomics once volume EM acquisition is in hand, so any reduction in merge errors would cut proofreading labor.
ocar.challenge: Conventional chemical fixation collapses extracellular space, packing membranes so tightly that algorithms merge neighboring neurites; over-segmentation then leaves many fragments to reassemble.
ocar.action: Pallotto, Watkins, Briggman and colleagues preserved extracellular space (ECS) during chemical fixation and measured machine-learning segmentation error, electrical-synapse visibility, and antibody penetration as functions of ECS volume fraction.
ocar.resolution: ECS-preserved tissue segmented with significantly reduced error rates. Modest fractions of 6% already improved performance versus typical <1% after standard perfusion; further increases did not keep helping because cells, especially glial sheets, shrank. Electrical synapses were readily identified, and antibodies penetrated deeply with only minimal permeabilization, enabling correlated light and EM.
ocar.future_work: The authors emphasize they were optimizing an analysis artifact, not in-vivo-like ECS (freezing is cited as the route to that), and that an optimal ECS fraction balances neurite separation against process shrinkage.

summaries.beginner: Brain tissue usually collapses when it is chemically fixed, so nerve-cell membranes stick together and computers merge the wrong cells. This paper keeps a little space between cells on purpose, which makes automatic tracing easier and also helps antibodies and gap-junction synapses show up.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2015), Pallotto, Watkins, Singer, and Briggman show that preserving extracellular space during chemical fixation improves connectomic analysis. Segmentation error fell relative to standard dense packing; 6% ECS already helped versus <1%, with diminishing returns at higher fractions because of cellular shrinkage. Gap junctions were easier to see, and antibody penetration with minimal permeabilization supported correlated LM/EM. The goal was better images for algorithms, not faithful in-vivo extracellular geometry.
summaries.advanced: The paper does not claim in-vivo ECS volume fractions; freeze substitution is explicitly preferred for morphology. Segmentation gains are reported as significant with an apparent optimum, but the extracted discussion does not give a single summary error-rate table. Applicability is argued generally for neuropil; circuit-specific reconstructions are not the main result. Merge-error reduction is expected to cut proofreading, not eliminate it.

plain_language_summary: Brain tissue usually collapses when it is chemically fixed, so nerve-cell membranes stick together and computers merge the wrong cells. This paper keeps a little space between cells on purpose, which makes automatic tracing easier and also helps antibodies and gap-junction synapses show up.

ocar.opportunity: Dense 3D EM connectomics needs homogeneous heavy-metal staining throughout every neurite and synapse in a large block, which would also relax how precisely a functionally imaged region must be targeted.
ocar.challenge: Existing en-bloc protocols either produced prohibitive staining gradients beyond typical ~100–200 μm penetration or stained only a subset of neurites (e.g., myelin) and required charge compensation; whole-brain protocols can take months.
ocar.action: Hua, Laserstein, and Helmstaedter altered osmium tetroxide and uranyl acetate impregnation, guided by OsO4 membrane chemistry (including OsO2 deposition and temperature-dependent uranyl acetate diffusion versus reactivity), to stain large mouse neocortex blocks.
ocar.resolution: The protocol provided high-contrast full-neuropil staining for densely reconstructable mouse neocortex blocks at least 1 mm in diameter, on a days-scale rather than months-scale process.
ocar.future_work: By relaxing topographic targeting constraints, the authors argue correlated functional and structural circuit analysis becomes realistic at these block sizes.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope stains often fail to reach the middle of a large piece of brain, so only tiny blocks could be mapped. This paper describes a faster way to stain mouse cortex all the way through a millimeter-wide chunk so every wire can be seen.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2015), Hua, Laserstein, and Helmstaedter report a large-volume dense en-bloc EM staining protocol for mouse neocortex. Classic protocols were limited to roughly 100–200 μm penetration or to myelinated fibers. Building on OsO4–lipid chemistry and colder uranyl acetate to favor diffusion over reactivity, they obtain high-contrast, full-neuropil staining in blocks at least 1 mm across. The stated aim is to make correlated physiology and dense reconstruction practical.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract is strongest on chemical rationale (OTO versus reducing-agent pathways, Os oxidation states) and the 1 mm diameter claim; quantitative contrast-versus-depth curves are referred to figures not fully captured in the extract. “Densely reconstructable” is a staining/contrast claim, not a published complete cortical column connectome in this paper. Comparison to the months-scale whole-brain protocol is qualitative.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope stains often fail to reach the middle of a large piece of brain, so only tiny blocks could be mapped. This paper describes a faster way to stain mouse cortex all the way through a millimeter-wide chunk so every wire can be seen.

ocar.opportunity: Expert tracers use neuron- and circuit-scale context that purely local machine vision lacks, so building that context into proofreading could replace expensive independent reconstructions.
ocar.challenge: Electron-microscopy circuit mapping is slow and error-prone; combining multiple independent reconstructions multiplies labor, while algorithms using only local membranes are sensitive to noise, especially in anisotropic serial sections.
ocar.action: Schneider-Mizell, Gerhard, Cardona and colleagues added quantitative arbor and network measures to CATMAID and applied them iteratively in Drosophila larva sensorimotor and adult visual reconstructions.
ocar.resolution: Synaptic inputs sat preferentially on microtubule-free “twigs” off a microtubule-rich “backbone”; omitting individual twigs accounted for 96% of errors, yet strong connections spread synapses across many twigs, coupling anatomical robustness to reconstruction robustness. Iterative, context-guided reconstruction matched or beat multi-reconstruction consensus without redundant full tracing.
ocar.future_work: They estimate graph-topology error from random twig omission and discuss false-edge probabilities on motor neurons, framing focused checks on weak edges as the remaining risk.

summaries.beginner: When people trace fly neurons in electron-microscope stacks, most mistakes are missing tiny side branches, not the main trunk. This paper shows that strong connections usually use many of those twigs, so a careful, anatomy-aware tracing method can skip doing the same cell three times.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2016), Schneider-Mizell, Gerhard, Cardona and colleagues describe iterative proofreading in CATMAID guided by quantitative neuroanatomy. In Drosophila, a microtubule-containing backbone carries most presynaptic sites, while postsynaptic inputs concentrate on small microtubule-free twigs. Twig omissions were 96% of errors; numerically strong edges distributed synapses across twigs. Comparing iterative reconstruction to multi-annotator consensus, they argue redundant independent tracing is unnecessary if arbor and network context are used.
summaries.advanced: The catalog lists this as bioRxiv (2015); the selected PDF is the eLife article (published 18 March 2016). The 96% figure is for omission of individual twigs as a share of errors, not overall synapse precision. False-positive edge models (e.g., m = 5, 20, 37 false inputs) are scenario calculations from validation data. Findings are tied to Drosophila stereotypy and may not transfer unchanged to mammalian dendrites.

plain_language_summary: When people trace fly neurons in electron-microscope stacks, most mistakes are missing tiny side branches, not the main trunk. This paper shows that strong connections usually use many of those twigs, so a careful, anatomy-aware tracing method can skip doing the same cell three times.

ocar.opportunity: A saturated, minable reconstruction of all cells and many organelles in a neocortical volume would let many questions be asked of one dataset, analogous to a genome without prior functional focus.
ocar.challenge: Whether physical proximity of axons and dendritic spines is enough to predict excitatory synapses (Peters’ rule) was still contested, and prior studies had not scored every touching axon against every spine in a volume.
ocar.action: Kasthuri, Lichtman and colleagues built a tape-based EM pipeline and generated a saturated reconstruction of a mouse neocortex sub-volume, itemizing cellular objects and subcellular components including an annotated database of 1,700 synapses.
ocar.resolution: Each spine was closely apposed by about nine axons, typically only one of which synapsed. An axon that already synapsed on a dendrite had a 40% chance of another synapse on the same dendrite, versus about 1.6% for axons that only touched; proximity was necessary but not sufficient, refuting Peters’ rule for these excitatory spine synapses.
ocar.future_work: Images, visualization/editing tools, and analysis code were released via the Open Connectome Project for further queries of the same volume.

summaries.beginner: This team used a tape-collection electron-microscope pipeline to catalog every cell process and 1,700 synapses in a bit of mouse cortex. They show that an axon sitting next to a spine is not enough to predict a connection—cells seem choosier than that.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell (2015), Kasthuri et al. report automated nanometer-scale technologies and a saturated reconstruction of mouse neocortex, with axons, dendrites, glia, synapses, vesicles, spines, and mitochondria itemized. Highlights include a database of 1,700 synapses. Scoring every excitatory axon–spine juxtaposition, they find about nine nearby axons per spine, usually one synapse, and a 40% versus ~1.6% repeat-synapse probability depending on whether the axon already innervated that dendrite—evidence against Peters’ rule.
summaries.advanced: There were no antecedent functional recordings by design; inferences are structural. The 40% and ~1.6% figures apply to excitatory axon–spine relationships in this volume, not to inhibitory or other synapse classes. “Saturated” refers to the reconstructed sub-volume, not a whole cortical column. Data-access URLs in the paper (openconnecto.me) may have moved since 2015.

plain_language_summary: This team used a tape-collection electron-microscope pipeline to catalog every cell process and 1,700 synapses in a bit of mouse cortex. They show that an axon sitting next to a spine is not enough to predict a connection—cells seem choosier than that.

ocar.opportunity: FIB-SEM can deliver isotropic volumes below 10 × 10 × 10 nm that are well suited to automatic tracing, but the millable chunk size is poorly matched to larger tissue blocks.
ocar.challenge: Ion milling is a “soft knife” optimized for nanometer surface removal, not for subdividing millimeter-scale samples into parallelizable pieces without destroying ultrastructure at the cut.
ocar.action: Hayworth, Xu, Hess and colleagues developed ultrathick sectioning (hot-knife partitioning) that cuts embedded tissue into ~20 μm chunks mounted for efficient parallel FIB-SEM, then volume-stitches the stacks.
ocar.resolution: Stitched volumes were judged suitable for connectome tracing. Image-mismatch at the hot-knife plane was comparable to a ~40 nm gap in a faux TEM stack for mouse cortex (mismatch 5.3 vs 5.2) and ~30 nm equivalent for C-PLT Drosophila tissue.
ocar.future_work: The method is presented as a route to larger-scale FIB-SEM connectomics by parallelizing many optimally sized chunks.

summaries.beginner: The best 3D electron microscopes can shave tissue only a few nanometers at a time, so big samples have to be cut into slabs first. This paper shows how to make those slabs about 20 micrometers thick with a heated knife and then digitally glue the pictures back into one volume.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2015), Hayworth et al. introduce ultrathick sectioning and volume stitching for FIB-SEM. Embedded samples are partitioned into ~20 μm chunks for parallel imaging at better than 10 nm isotropic sampling, then stitched. For cortex, hot-knife image mismatch matched a simulated 40 nm gap; for C-PLT fly tissue a polynomial fit equated the jump to about 30 nm removed. Custom FIB-SEMs and control software at Janelia underpinned the work.
summaries.advanced: Gap equivalence is an image-correlation proxy (Gaussian-filtered absolute pixel difference), not a claim that no neurites are lost. Tracing suitability is asserted; the extract does not report a full connectome error rate across stitches. Early methods development involved multiple labs’ tissues (cortex, larva, high-pressure-frozen samples). Authors note no competing financial interests in the manuscript.

plain_language_summary: The best 3D electron microscopes can shave tissue only a few nanometers at a time, so big samples have to be cut into slabs first. This paper shows how to make those slabs about 20 micrometers thick with a heated knife and then digitally glue the pictures back into one volume.

ocar.opportunity: Aside from the C. elegans microscale connectome, vertebrate brains lacked a complete, standardized, brain-wide connectivity dataset at cellular/mesoscale resolution.
ocar.challenge: Projection mapping across animals is hard to compare without a common 3D atlas, unbiased tracers, and high-throughput whole-brain imaging.
ocar.action: Oh, Harris, Ng, Zeng and colleagues built the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas using EGFP-expressing AAV tracers from defined regions and cell types, serial two-photon tomography, registration to a common 3D space, and network modeling.
ocar.resolution: The pipeline produced a whole-brain connectivity matrix. Duplicate experiments correlated on average 0.90 across 12 sets. Ipsilateral and corresponding contralateral projections were similar (Pearson’s r = 0.595) with weaker contralateral strengths. Connection weights were lognormal; the brain showed small-world and scale-free features without fitting either model alone. Cortico-thalamic analyses illustrated segregation and integration of parallel pathways.
ocar.future_work: Phase I regional coverage was not fully redundant, AAV tropism might be incomplete, and cytoplasmic EGFP matrices include false positives from artifacts and injection-tract contamination; the atlas is framed as a first systematic step.

summaries.beginner: This project traces outgoing axons from many starting points in the mouse brain and lines all the experiments up in one 3D map. The result is a public wiring atlas of regional connections, not a synapse-by-synapse diagram.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2014), the Allen Institute reports a mesoscale mouse connectome: EGFP AAV anterograde tracing, serial two-photon tomography, and informatic registration into a common volume (connectivity.brain-map.org). A computational model addresses strength distributions, symmetry, and network statistics; virtual tractography shows 3D topography. Average correlation 0.90 in 12 duplicate sets supports consistency. Cortico-thalamic pathways exemplify segregation and integration.
summaries.advanced: This is cellular-level mesoscale projection mapping, not EM synaptic resolution—the C. elegans comparison in the abstract is about completeness of a wiring dataset, not matching scale. The matrix can contain false positives (tissue/imaging artifacts, injection tracts). AAV promoter/serotype bias is not excluded. Catalog metadata that tag this record as C. elegans are inconsistent with the paper, which is mouse.

plain_language_summary: This project traces outgoing axons from many starting points in the mouse brain and lines all the experiments up in one 3D map. The result is a public wiring atlas of regional connections, not a synapse-by-synapse diagram.

ocar.opportunity: A complete sensory-to-motor wiring diagram plus behavior can show how spatial light differences become coordinated movement, a possible intermediate toward image-forming vision.
ocar.challenge: How light inputs translate into motor output during visual navigation was poorly understood, and no synaptic-level map spanning photoreceptors, interneurons, and motorneurons for a visual circuit was available.
ocar.action: Randel, Jékely and colleagues reconstructed a 71-neuron four-eye visual circuit in a Platynereis dumerilii larva with serial-section TEM, and combined eye ablations with phototaxis assays.
ocar.resolution: Photoreceptors connect through three interneuron layers to trunk-muscle motorneurons. The circuit compares left–right light and drives bending on imbalance. Spatial vision depends on at least two differently aimed eyes, not on multiple photoreceptors within one eye (those share a primary interneuron). Crosswise eye modules and an interneuron motif enhance contrast; a bilateral eye pair elicits a smaller motor response than a crosswise pair at the same intensity contrast.
ocar.future_work: The authors note it is not yet possible to link every neuron and synapse to phototactic behavior; reconstructions partly explain positive versus negative phototaxis switching.

summaries.beginner: A marine worm larva has four simple eyes and can swim toward or away from light. This paper maps the 71 nerve cells from those eyes to the swimming muscles and shows the animal compares brightness on the two sides of its body.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2014), Randel et al. reconstruct the Platynereis larval visual circuit with ssTEM (71 neurons) and test function with laser eye ablations. Photoreceptors of one eye converge on the same primary interneuron, so spatial vision requires multiple eyes. Downstream circuitry is point-symmetric and crosswise; contrast enhancement occurs in the primary optic neuropil. The circuit has spatial detection and contrast modulation, framed as an evolutionary intermediate that contrasts light versus dark fields.
summaries.advanced: Completeness is claimed for this four-eye visual circuit in one larva, not the entire nervous system. Linking every connection to behavior is explicitly incomplete. Phototaxis polarity (positive vs negative) is only partly explained. Eye photoreceptor counts in the studied larva are given as 2–7 per eye in the introduction; all photoreceptors of one eye share a primary interneuron.

plain_language_summary: A marine worm larva has four simple eyes and can swim toward or away from light. This paper maps the 71 nerve cells from those eyes to the swimming muscles and shows the animal compares brightness on the two sides of its body.

ocar.opportunity: How the mammalian retina detects motion had remained open for about 50 years; a connectomic look at starburst amacrine cells (SACs) and bipolar cells (BCs) could supply a wiring clue.
ocar.challenge: Physiological models needed anatomical evidence that different bipolar types contact SAC dendrites at different distances from the soma, matching known differences in visual-response timing.
ocar.action: Kim, Greene, Seung, Denk and colleagues, with EyeWire citizen neuroscientists, reconstructed Off-type SACs and BCs from serial EM (dataset e2198), scored contact area and branch depth, and tested a mathematical space–time wiring model.
ocar.resolution: One BC type preferred to wire near the SAC soma and another far from it; the near type is known to lag the far type. The model shows how that specificity could orient SAC dendritic receptive fields in space–time and favor outward (centrifugal) motion. Seventy-nine Off SACs were reconstructed (more than half the estimated population in e2198); after a “Starburst Challenge,” EyeWirers needed GrimReaper correction on only 8% of SAC cubes.
ocar.future_work: Off BC somata were generally outside the volume, so axons were followed from the inner nuclear layer; confirmation of the model’s physiological predictions remains for functional work.

summaries.beginner: How the eye spots movement has been a puzzle for decades. Volunteers on EyeWire helped trace starburst cells and bipolar cells, and the wiring pattern looks like a delay line: some inputs arrive farther out on the branch and earlier in time, which can make the branch prefer motion away from the cell body.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2014), Kim et al. reconstruct Off SACs and bipolar cells in serial EM with EyeWire. Contact and co-stratification analyses indicate one BC type prefers proximal SAC dendrite and another distal; the proximal type lags in time. A model shows space–time wiring specificity can yield outward direction selectivity. Reconstruction mixed lab workers and EyeWirers (79 Off SACs; overlapping forward/backward and worker/EyeWirer counts are reported). Denk discloses SBEM license income from Gatan.
summaries.advanced: Direction selectivity is inferred from anatomy plus a model and known BC kinetics, not from paired physiology in this volume. SAC identification used morphological criteria (IPL depth, starburst shape); forward candidates were >90% SACs, backward <25%. BC axons were hard to reconstruct; cells violating known BC structure were discarded as amacrine cells. The classic 50-year problem is not claimed solved by physiology in this paper.

plain_language_summary: How the eye spots movement has been a puzzle for decades. Volunteers on EyeWire helped trace starburst cells and bipolar cells, and the wiring pattern looks like a delay line: some inputs arrive farther out on the branch and earlier in time, which can make the branch prefer motion away from the cell body.

ocar.opportunity: Neuroanatomy is now large-scale and quantitative, so researchers need interoperable tools to read, register, visualize, cluster, and graph-analyze neurons across whole brains and imaging modalities.
ocar.challenge: Existing toolboxes often stop at simple morphometrics on isolated neurons, force custom code for repeated analyses, and do not compare morphology and connectivity after co-registration in a common template.
ocar.action: Bates, Manton, Jefferis and colleagues built the natverse, a suite of open-source R packages for local and remote neuron data, template bridging and mirroring, and integration of Drosophila light-microscopy and EM connectomic datasets.
ocar.resolution: The natverse supports visualization, clustering, graph-theoretic branching analysis, and transformations between template spaces. The authors demonstrate tools covering the vast majority of Drosophila neuroanatomical LM and EM datasets and deposit bridging/mirroring registrations in version-controlled GitHub repositories.
ocar.future_work: The suite is framed as an open platform for the community to add packages; the selected PDF is a 7 November 2019 bioRxiv version.

summaries.beginner: Fly brain maps now come from many labs and many microscopes, which makes comparing neurons a hassle. This software collection in R lines those maps up in shared templates so you can analyze shape and connections together.
summaries.intermediate: This bioRxiv preprint (version posted 7 November 2019) introduces the natverse: interoperable R packages for reading neuron data, visualization, clustering, graph analysis of arbors, and bridging between Drosophila template brains and imaging modalities, including EM connectomes. Unlike tools focused on isolated morphometrics, it emphasizes neurons in whole-brain context. Registrations are versioned on GitHub under jefferislab.
summaries.advanced: The catalog year is 2014; the selected PDF is the 2019 preprint. This is a methods/software paper, not a new connectome. Claims of covering the vast majority of Drosophila LM and EM datasets are authors’ demonstrations, not an independent audit in the extract. Users still need R literacy; the paper’s pitch is reduced environment-switching, not zero code.

plain_language_summary: Fly brain maps now come from many labs and many microscopes, which makes comparing neurons a hassle. This software collection in R lines those maps up in shared templates so you can analyze shape and connections together.

ocar.opportunity: Local motion detection in insect vision is thought to compare signals offset in space and time, but without a medulla connectome the cellular implementation remained elusive.
ocar.challenge: Intensive behavioral, physiological, and anatomical work had not identified which medulla cell types form the two arms of a correlation-type detector.
ocar.action: Takemura, Chklovskii, Meinertzhagen and colleagues developed a semi-automated EM pipeline and reconstructed a Drosophila optic medulla volume containing 379 neurons and 8,637 chemical synaptic contacts, matching cells to light-microscopy types.
ocar.resolution: Within the repeating medulla module they identified a candidate motion circuit: Mi1 and Tm3 as inputs to T4, with connection geometry consistent with T4 direction selectivity. They predict which arm should introduce a longer delay given synaptic polarities. Analogous L2-pathway candidates (Tm1, Tm2, Tm4) are suggested pending T5 reconstruction in the lobula.
ocar.future_work: Anatomy cannot probe the nonlinear operation or time delay needed to distinguish correlation models; T5/lobula confirmation is left explicit.

summaries.beginner: Flies see motion with a repeating column of cells behind the eye, but which cells do the comparison was unknown. This paper maps thousands of synapses in that column and points to a short list of cell types that look like a motion detector.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2013), Takemura et al. reconstruct Drosophila medulla connectome modules (379 neurons; 8,637 chemical synapses) with a semi-automated EM pipeline and light-microscopy type matching. Mi1 and Tm3 onto T4 are proposed as the two arms of a correlation-based detector; Tm3 had been easy to miss from arbor overlap in stratum M10. Comprehensiveness is used to argue both pathway importance and absence of alternatives. Parallels to vertebrate direction-selective ganglion cells and starburst amacrine cells are discussed with differences in preferred-direction geometry.
summaries.advanced: This is chemical synapses in medulla, not a full optic-lobe connectome including T5. Direction selectivity of T4 is aligned with dendritic orientation but preferred direction is away from dendritic tips, unlike SACs. Model class (Hassenstein–Reichardt versus others) cannot be chosen from anatomy alone. Sparse overlap-based connectivity estimates are argued to be inferior to synaptic counts.

plain_language_summary: Flies see motion with a repeating column of cells behind the eye, but which cells do the comparison was unknown. This paper maps thousands of synapses in that column and points to a short list of cell types that look like a motion detector.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can now acquire circuits of a few hundred to a few thousand neurons, so cellular-resolution connectomics is limited less by imaging than by turning those volumes into graphs.
ocar.challenge: Neuronal networks are high-dimensional graphs packed at extreme density in 3D tissue; comprehensively mapping them is a major challenge, and data analysis was massively lagging acquisition.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter’s perspective aims to summarize and quantify data-analysis challenges in cellular-resolution connectomics and to describe then-current solutions based on online crowd-sourcing and machine learning.
ocar.resolution: The piece frames dense reconstruction as an analysis-scale problem once volume EM data exist for circuits of hundreds to thousands of neurons, and it points to crowd and algorithmic approaches as the practical responses.
ocar.future_work: Closing the analysis gap is presented as the central remaining task for cellular-resolution connectomics.

summaries.beginner: Taking the pictures for a brain wiring map is getting easier; turning those pictures into a list of who talks to whom is the hard part. This perspective explains why tracing densely packed neurons at cellular resolution is so demanding and how crowds and machine learning were being used to catch up.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2013), Moritz Helmstaedter reviews cellular-resolution connectomics as a data-analysis problem. Volume EM had made acquisition feasible for circuits of a few hundred to a few thousand neurons, but analysis lagged. The perspective sets out to quantify those challenges and to describe online crowd-sourcing and machine-learning approaches then in use.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract does not match this article (it is a 2026 Molecules review on fluorescent labeling). This card therefore uses only the catalog abstract. No original reconstructions, error rates, or software benchmarks should be inferred beyond what the abstract states. It is a perspective, not an empirical methods paper.

plain_language_summary: Taking the pictures for a brain wiring map is getting easier; turning those pictures into a list of who talks to whom is the hard part. This perspective explains why tracing densely packed neurons at cellular resolution is so demanding and how crowds and machine learning were being used to catch up.

ocar.opportunity: The inner plexiform layer is the retina’s main computational neuropil, so a dense map of neurons and contacts can test whether co-stratification predicts connectivity and can generate functional hypotheses.
ocar.challenge: High resolution and large extent are both required; fully manual labeling of the volume was estimated at about US$10 million, and automated segmentation still fragmented cells even at few-percent voxel error.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter, Briggman, Seung, Denk and colleagues applied crowd-sourced skeletons plus machine-learning volume segmentation to serial block-face EM dataset e2006 (>1 million μm³), covering layers with intra-retinal synapses and stained for plasma-membrane contrast.
ocar.resolution: They densely reconstructed 950 neurons and their mutual contacts, confirmed ten known bipolar types, discovered the XBC, and subdivided a known type by connectivity. Motifs suggested a mechanism for localized-motion detection in one ganglion cell and predicted motion sensitivity in another. Contact could be used to augment type classification; neurite co-stratification did not always predict contact.
ocar.future_work: The functional role of the sparse, sharp-stratifying XBC remains unclear (possible luminance adaptation is speculated); an OFF-side cell with similarly sharp stratification was not found.

summaries.beginner: This team mapped 950 nerve cells in the mouse retina’s inner computing layer with a 3D electron microscope, volunteers, and computer vision. They found a new bipolar cell type and used the wiring pattern to guess how some ganglion cells detect motion.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2013), Helmstaedter et al. densely reconstruct the mouse inner plexiform layer from SBEM (e2006, more than 1 million μm³) using crowd-sourced annotation and ML segmentation. They report 950 neurons and contacts, a new bipolar type (XBC), connectivity-based splitting of a known type, and circuit motifs tied to a localized-motion ganglion cell plus a predicted motion-sensitive ganglion cell. SBEM’s z-resolution and low distortion are cited as aiding humans and computers. Peters-style inference from proximity is treated as frequently violated.
summaries.advanced: “Dense” refers to this IPL-centered volume, not the entire retina. Completely automatic reconstruction was not achieved; skeletons supply long-range continuity while segmented contacts supply area. The ~US$10 million fully manual cost is an estimate used to motivate the hybrid pipeline. XBC homology to primate giant bipolar cells is considered and argued against because of small dendritic fields. Contact-area percentages in figures (e.g., ON/OFF SAC) should be read from the paper’s panels rather than over-generalized.

plain_language_summary: This team mapped 950 nerve cells in the mouse retina’s inner computing layer with a 3D electron microscope, volunteers, and computer vision. They found a new bipolar cell type and used the wiring pattern to guess how some ganglion cells detect motion.

ocar.opportunity: Small invertebrate circuits whose connectivity is already known can teach what else is required to go from a wiring diagram to function, informing how to study large vertebrate circuits.
ocar.challenge: A connectome by itself does not specify dynamics, neuromodulation, or which of several parallel circuits is in use.
ocar.action: Bargmann and Marder, in a historical perspective, review invertebrate circuits with known connectivity and compare them with the vertebrate retina.
ocar.resolution: They highlight neuronal dynamics, neuromodulation, and parallel circuits as necessary ingredients beyond connectivity, argue that the retina shares these features, and suggest approaches for large circuits based on knowledge of small ones.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a conceptual program for studying functional organization, not a new reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: A complete list of who is connected to whom is not enough to know what a nervous system will do. This perspective uses well-mapped small animal circuits—and the retina—to argue that timing, chemical modulators, and spare parallel pathways also matter.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2013), Bargmann and Marder ask what information beyond connectivity diagrams is needed to understand nervous-system function. Drawing on invertebrate circuits with known wiring, they emphasize neuronal dynamics, neuromodulation, and parallel circuits. They note that the vertebrate retina shares these properties, suggesting generality, and they outline how lessons from small circuits might scale to large ones.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract does not match this article (it is a 2026 European Journal of Neuroscience paper on engrams and reductionism). This card therefore uses only the catalog abstract. No new empirical connectome or quantitative comparison is claimed. Catalog tags linking the record to mouse retina describe the comparison case in the abstract, not a retinal reconstruction by these authors.

plain_language_summary: A complete list of who is connected to whom is not enough to know what a nervous system will do. This perspective uses well-mapped small animal circuits—and the retina—to argue that timing, chemical modulators, and spare parallel pathways also matter.

ocar.opportunity: Graph measures from human neuroimaging suggested rich-club organization; a complete cellular connectome can test whether the same cost–value tradeoff appears at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: Most brain-network topology work used large-scale neuroimaging without cellular resolution, so it was unclear whether rich clubs were a general, scale-invariant principle.
ocar.action: Towlson, Vértes, Ahnert, Schafer, and Bullmore applied graph theory to the C. elegans neuronal connectome treated as 2,287 synaptic connections among 279 neurons.
ocar.resolution: An 11-neuron rich club (conservative 3σ definition) was highly efficient, long-distance, and almost entirely locomotor command interneurons (10 of 11), with DVA the remaining proprioceptive modulator. Rich-club cells are connector hubs; shortest paths between peripheral neurons most often traverse the club. Those neurons are born early, before visible movement and body elongation. Network efficiency was 47% of maximum at 4% connection density.
ocar.future_work: A more liberal club adds a few head interneurons (AIBR, RIBL, RIAR); the authors interpret high wiring cost as justified by coordinated movement, paralleling human imaging.

summaries.beginner: In the worm’s tiny nervous system, a handful of highly connected cells form a “rich club” that other cells use as a shortcut. Those club members are mostly the command cells for crawling, and they appear early in development.
summaries.intermediate: In the Journal of Neuroscience (2013), Towlson et al. analyze C. elegans as a graph of 279 neurons and 2,287 synapses. They identify an 11-node rich club with high efficiency, high betweenness, high participation, and relatively long physical connection distance. Ten of eleven conservative club members are locomotor command interneurons; DVA is proprioceptive. The connectome is small-world (Watts–Strogatz) with efficiency 47% of maximum at 4% density, and wiring cost is strongly but not strictly minimized.
summaries.advanced: The analysis is uninformed by prior functional labels yet recovers locomotor interneurons—an alignment, not an independent causal test. Synaptic connections are treated as undirected/unweighted in the simple graphical model described. Laser-ablation literature is cited for function, not re-done here. Human neuroimaging parallels are analogical across scale.

plain_language_summary: In the worm’s tiny nervous system, a handful of highly connected cells form a “rich club” that other cells use as a shortcut. Those club members are mostly the command cells for crawling, and they appear early in development.

ocar.opportunity: For Drosophila and C. elegans, image acquisition was no longer the limiting step; extracting circuits from terascale EM and optical volumes on desktop hardware was.
ocar.challenge: Laboratories needed open tools to compose deformed serial tiles into browsable volumes, reconstruct arbors, annotate synapses, and manage huge image and annotation collections.
ocar.action: Cardona, Saalfeld, Douglas and colleagues built TrakEM2, an open-source package for volume composition, fast manual and semi-automatic arbor and synapse annotation, and export of 3D circuits in NeuroML and other formats.
ocar.resolution: The software had already been used for Drosophila larval CNS EM, array tomography, LSM lineage reconstruction, cat thalamocortical connections, and an inhibitory network in a 10-terabyte mouse visual-cortex EM set, among other projects. Sketching types (balls, pipes, connectors, area lists) support synapses and vesicle counts.
ocar.future_work: The output is framed as analysis-ready circuit structure rather than a finished biological connectome in this methods paper.

summaries.beginner: Huge stacks of electron-microscope pictures are useless until someone traces the cells. TrakEM2 is a free program that stitches those pictures, lets people draw neurons and synapses, and exports a 3D wiring sketch.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS ONE (2012), Cardona et al. present TrakEM2 for neural circuit reconstruction from large EM and optical volumes. It targets image-volume composition from deformed tiles, arbor reconstruction, synapse annotation, and management of tera-scale collections on consumer computers. Demonstrated uses include Drosophila larval CNS, array tomography, optical lineage work, cat visual cortex, and a 10 TB mouse visual-cortex inhibitory-network reconstruction. Export includes NeuroML.
summaries.advanced: This is software and workflow, not a new complete connectome; biological results live in the cited applications. Catalog organism/dataset tags pointing at C. elegans reflect the paper’s motivating model systems, not a worm reconstruction in this article. Performance claims are qualitative (expeditious reconstruction) without benchmark tables in the extracted text.

plain_language_summary: Huge stacks of electron-microscope pictures are useless until someone traces the cells. TrakEM2 is a free program that stitches those pictures, lets people draw neurons and synapses, and exports a 3D wiring sketch.

ocar.opportunity: New SEM methods and scaled, automated TEM made large EM volumes newly available for extracting neuronal wiring diagrams.
ocar.challenge: There is no single best volume-EM method: size, resolution, completeness, speed, and reliability trade off, and dendrite spine necks (~40 nm) or Drosophila neurites (~50 nm) set resolution needs, while a mouse cortical column is ~100 times an adult C. elegans volume.
ocar.action: Briggman and Bock review volume EM acquisition methods, their tradeoffs, and applicability to anatomical connectivity, arguing that wiring diagrams are necessary but not sufficient.
ocar.resolution: They conclude volume EM is best combined with molecular biology, optogenetics, and physiology. In the short term, sparse reconstruction of subsets of connections will keep yielding insight; dense mammalian millimeter-scale reconstruction awaits analysis automation. Data analysis times already dwarf acquisition for complete dense reconstruction.
ocar.future_work: They anticipate that progress in automating acquisition will carry over to analysis, eventually permitting complete mammalian circuit reconstruction across millimeter scales.

summaries.beginner: Scientists now have several ways to take 3D electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue, each with different speed and sharpness. This review says those pictures can give a wiring diagram, but you still need other tools—genes, light, and electrical recordings—to understand what the circuit does.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2012), Briggman and Bock survey SEM and TEM volume methods for circuit reconstruction. Required volume depends on the circuit (adult C. elegans ~50 × 50 × 1000 μm versus a mouse cortical column ~400 × 400 × 1000 μm). Voxel size must follow the finest processes (mammalian spine necks as fine as 40 nm; Drosophila neurites as thin as 50 nm). Completeness matters because lost sections mix thin processes. They argue connectomes are necessary but not sufficient without multimodal physiology.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/opinion, not a new dataset. Cited TEMCA volume (450 × 350 × 50 μm) is from Bock et al. 2011, used as an example of combined two-photon and EM. “No best method” is the explicit stance. Dense millimeter-scale mammalian reconstruction is a projected future, not a result.

plain_language_summary: Scientists now have several ways to take 3D electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue, each with different speed and sharpness. This review says those pictures can give a wiring diagram, but you still need other tools—genes, light, and electrical recordings—to understand what the circuit does.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM can image densely stained neuropil fast enough that reconstruction, not acquisition, limits connectome throughput.
ocar.challenge: In dense data even experts err, especially at branches; a missed branch can misattribute thousands of synapses, and conventional proofreading of skeletons is tiresome.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter, Briggman, and Denk introduced KNOSSOS for rapid manual skeletonization (~50-fold faster than volume labeling) and RESCOP, a redundant-skeleton consensus procedure with a statistical model of annotation decisions.
ocar.resolution: RESCOP detects inconsistencies across redundant skeletons, estimates consensus reliability, and supports focused re-annotation of difficult locations (vote ratios near 0.5 are rare). Annotators without prior neurobiology knowledge can be used if redundancy and focused review are applied. The optimal vote threshold can differ from majority voting.
ocar.future_work: Error-rate estimates for large redundancy N are somewhat uncertain because difficult locations are rare; the assumption that infinite annotators converge to truth limits ultimate validity.

summaries.beginner: When every nerve fiber is stained, even experts mix up branches. This paper has people quickly draw stick-figure traces of the same cell several times, then a statistical method (RESCOP) votes out the mistakes much faster than painting every voxel.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2011), Helmstaedter, Briggman, and Denk present KNOSSOS skeletonization and RESCOP consensus for densely labeled SBEM data. Manual skeletons are ~50 times faster than volume labeling. Redundant traces plus a model of how true continuity becomes votes yield consensus skeletons and reliability estimates. Focused re-annotation of ambiguous sites is predicted to raise reliability steeply with average redundancy. Neurite continuity errors are treated as far more costly than single synapse-ID errors.
summaries.advanced: The ~50-fold speedup is versus volume labeling, not versus later machine segmentation. Expert errors at branches are demonstrated; synapse identification errors are acknowledged but not the main quantification. Infinite-annotator convergence is an explicit limiting assumption. Denk/Helmstaedter disclose patent and SBEM license income. Sparse Golgi-like data are described as assumed reliable with little published validation.

plain_language_summary: When every nerve fiber is stained, even experts mix up branches. This paper has people quickly draw stick-figure traces of the same cell several times, then a statistical method (RESCOP) votes out the mistakes much faster than painting every voxel.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical wiring diagrams are incomplete without knowing each neuron’s function; combining in-vivo physiology with network anatomy can test how geometry and tuning shape connections.
ocar.challenge: Past synaptic studies sampled few cells, so the structure of highly interconnected cortical networks was only partially known.
ocar.action: Bock, Lee, Reid and colleagues measured preferred orientation in mouse V1 with two-photon calcium imaging, then used a custom TEM camera array (TEMCA) on serial thin sections to trace local axons of those pyramids and their postsynaptic targets.
ocar.resolution: Inhibitory interneurons received convergent anatomical input from nearby excitatory neurons spanning a broad range of preferred orientations, consistent with physiological predictions that inhibitory cells are less selective, although weak biases could not be rejected. In the sample, 51% of synapses were onto inhibitory targets. The imaged series was 350 × 450 μm wide and only 52 μm in the sectioning dimension, so only 245 of the thousands of synapses made by characterized neurons could be traced.
ocar.future_work: Larger EM volumes were anticipated; subtype-specific inhibitory selectivity was not classified and could still exist.

summaries.beginner: Researchers first watched mouse visual-cortex cells respond to oriented bars, then traced some of their connections in electron-microscope slices. Inhibitory cells collected input from neighbors that preferred many different orientations, which may help explain why those inhibitory cells are less picky.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2011), Bock et al. combine two-photon orientation mapping with large-scale serial-section EM (TEMCA) in mouse V1. Reconstructed pyramidal axons synapse onto inhibitory neurons with broadly distributed orientation preferences; strong bias is excluded, weak bias is not. 51% of sampled synapses were onto inhibitory targets, higher than 10–20% reports from cat and macaque, possibly species or proximal-axon sampling. The public volume is noted at Whole Brain Catalog and UCSD CCDB (MP8448).
summaries.advanced: Sampling is partial: 245 synapses from proximal arbors in a 52 μm-thick volume. Interneuron subtypes were not classified. Geometry appeared to dominate over function for excitatory-to-inhibitory connections in this analysis. The 51% inhibitory-target fraction should not be read as a whole-cortex synapse census. Alignment between in-vivo imaging and EM is a prerequisite that limits which cells enter the anatomical sample.

plain_language_summary: Researchers first watched mouse visual-cortex cells respond to oriented bars, then traced some of their connections in electron-microscope slices. Inhibitory cells collected input from neighbors that preferred many different orientations, which may help explain why those inhibitory cells are less picky.

ocar.opportunity: Direction-selective ganglion cells (DSGCs) compute motion direction, but the wiring that creates asymmetric inhibition from starburst amacrine cells (SACs) was unresolved at scale.
ocar.challenge: Light-microscopy proximity studies conflicted, and earlier EM could not reconstruct large fractions of SACs and DSGCs together; physiology alone cannot locate which SAC dendrite branches contact which DSGC.
ocar.action: Briggman, Helmstaedter, and Denk combined two-photon calcium imaging of DSGCs in mouse retina with serial block-face EM and targeted reconstructions of SAC–DSGC synapses.
ocar.resolution: SAC dendrites selectively synapse onto a DSGC when oriented along that cell’s null direction, providing a structural substrate for asymmetric inhibitory currents. Among 831 synapses, dendrite angle contributed beyond soma–soma geometry, consistent with SAC dendrites as independent computational units. Incidental touches (n = 3,481) were distinguished from synapses. Synapses occur across the DSGC field, so some strongly connected SAC somata can lie on the preferred side.
ocar.future_work: The same SBEM data are expected to support dense retinal circuit reconstruction; development must use local dendrite geometry or activity, not cell identity alone, to place synapses.

summaries.beginner: Some retinal cells fire only when a spot moves one way. This paper shows that starburst cells wire most strongly onto those motion cells along the opposite, “null” direction, which can shut them down when motion goes the wrong way.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2011), Briggman, Helmstaedter, and Denk pair two-photon calcium imaging (Oregon Green 488 BAPTA-1; bars in eight directions at 0.5 mm s⁻¹) with SBEM in C57BL/6 mouse retina. SAC-to-DSGC synapses (n = 831) follow null-direction dendrite orientation more than soma angle alone. The asymmetry supports models with null-direction inhibition and rules out purely symmetric wiring with only strength differences. SBEM is contrasted with artifact-prone serial-section EM.
summaries.advanced: Reconstructions are targeted, not a full IPL connectome (that is anticipated). Synapse versus touch classification is central (3,481 incidental touches). Preferred-direction excitation asymmetry is not the primary structural claim. Developmental mechanism is constrained, not identified. Motion speed and stimulus details in Methods Summary should not be generalized to all DSGC subtypes without the paper’s cell-class definitions.

plain_language_summary: Some retinal cells fire only when a spot moves one way. This paper shows that starburst cells wire most strongly onto those motion cells along the opposite, “null” direction, which can shut them down when motion goes the wrong way.

ocar.opportunity: Vertebrate synaptic circuits cannot be completed by unaided manual ssTEM, so automated reconstruction must be tested on real neuropil, and light-microscopy “potential synapse” rules need ultrastructural checks.
ocar.challenge: It was unclear when axo-dendritic proximity or membrane touches predict actual synapses, i.e., when Peters’ rule holds.
ocar.action: Mishchenko, Hu, Harris, Chklovskii and colleagues densely reconstructed four rat hippocampus volumes totaling 670 μm³ with automated ssTEM registration/segmentation plus RECONSTRUCT proofreading.
ocar.resolution: Axon density within reach of spines did not predict synaptic density because the fraction of axons that synapse varied. An axo-dendritic touch did not predict a synapse, yet synapse density was a universal fraction 0.2 of touch density along hippocampal dendrites. The largest bouton–spine touch predicted actual synapses with about 80% precision but would miss about half of synapses. Synaptic density scaled with dendrite caliber (universal shaft membrane area 0.66 μm² per synapse), not with local axon availability.
ocar.future_work: Proofreading speed and error rates were satisfactory for these small volumes but need radical improvement to reconstruct complete vertebrate circuits. Datasets lacking ultrastructural synapse cues will poorly predict connectivity.

summaries.beginner: In a bit of rat hippocampus, this team outlined every nearby axon and dendrite in electron-microscope slices. Simply sitting next to each other does not mean two cells are connected; you still need the synapse’s fine structure to tell a real contact from a near miss.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2010), Mishchenko et al. densely reconstruct 670 μm³ of rat hippocampal neuropil (four volumes) with automated ssTEM methods. Peters’ rule fails for predicting synaptic density from nearby axon density. Touches outnumber synapses; synapses are about 0.2 of touches along dendrites. Largest-touch inference is ~80% precise but misses about half of synapses. Caliber, not local axon crowding, correlates with synapse density (0.66 μm² shaft membrane per synapse).
summaries.advanced: Volumes are too small for complete circuits; they are proving grounds. Mean connectivity fraction matching light-microscopy theory coexists with enough dendrite-to-dendrite variation to break Peters’ rule. The 80%/50% largest-touch result cautions against LM or low-resolution EM connectivity inference. Catalog organism “other” is rat hippocampus in the paper.

plain_language_summary: In a bit of rat hippocampus, this team outlined every nearby axon and dendrite in electron-microscope slices. Simply sitting next to each other does not mean two cells are connected; you still need the synapse’s fine structure to tell a real contact from a near miss.

ocar.opportunity: Even for C. elegans, published wiring diagrams were neither accurate nor complete and self-consistent, yet statistical network properties might generalize if a cleaned map existed.
ocar.challenge: Prior assemblies made unjustified assumptions that some reconstructed neurons represented others, and analyses used incomplete or inconsistent diagrams.
ocar.action: Varshney, Chen, Hall, Chklovskii and colleagues assembled whole, self-consistent gap-junction and chemical-synapse networks of hermaphrodite C. elegans from White et al. materials plus new electron micrographs, then computed topology, motifs, linear-systems activity modes, and gap-versus-chemical interactions.
ocar.resolution: They propose a signal-flow visualization, identify central neurons and candidate functional motifs, find activity patterns that could underlie known behaviors, and note that multiplicity and motif statistics resemble mammalian neocortex. The diagram is meant to generate predictions for genetic perturbations, laser ablations, and activity monitoring.
ocar.future_work: Connectivity alone is stated as not sufficient to explain function; the resource is a substrate for experiments rather than a completed mechanistic account of behavior.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring list had gaps and inconsistencies. This paper rebuilds a coherent map of chemical synapses and gap junctions for the hermaphrodite and then asks what the network’s shape can tell us about signal flow and behavior.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2011), Varshney et al. curate self-consistent C. elegans hermaphrodite chemical and gap-junction networks from the White et al. archive and new EM. They report degree distributions, synaptic multiplicities, small-world properties, motifs, and eigenmodes of linear activity, plus statistical coupling between gap junctions and chemical synapses. Similarities to neocortical multiplicity/motif statistics are taken as candidate general principles.
summaries.advanced: The catalog year is 2009; the selected PDF is the 2011 PLoS Computational Biology article. Linear-systems “activity patterns” are models, not measured calcium or voltage. Completeness is relative to prior published diagrams, not a claim of zero remaining EM ambiguity. GABAergic-conditioned likelihood ratios for gap/chemical co-occurrence are in the supporting analysis, not a physiological proof of interaction rules.

ocar.opportunity: Completely reconstructing neuronal connectivity needs 3D tissue structure over hundreds of micrometers at a resolution that follows the thinnest processes and identifies synapses, a gap between conventional EM of tiny volumes and light microscopy.
ocar.challenge: Serial ultrathin TEM is laborious and hard to automate; SEM was mostly a surface tool; charging of uncoated block faces and sectioning chatter limit in-chamber imaging.
ocar.action: Denk and Horstmann combined automated diamond-knife serial sectioning inside an SEM with backscattered-electron imaging of heavy-metal-stained, TEM-style blocks under low vacuum (20–60 Pa H2O).
ocar.resolution: Resolution sufficed to trace the thinnest axons and identify synapses. Stacks of several hundred sections 50–70 nm thick were obtained with typical lateral position jitter under 10 nm, enabling automated EM-level 3D datasets without slice-to-slice distortion correction that needs manual landmarks.
ocar.future_work: They discuss thinner sections (toward ~20 nm), lower beam energies, oscillating knives, and nonmechanical ablation, while noting radiation damage and charging tradeoffs relative to TEM.

summaries.beginner: This paper shows how to put a tiny diamond knife inside a scanning electron microscope so the machine can shave a stained tissue block and photograph each new face automatically. The resulting 3D stack is sharp enough to follow the thinnest nerve fibers and see synapses.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology (2004), Denk and Horstmann introduce serial block-face SEM. Backscattered electrons image routine heavy-metal stains; 20–60 Pa water vapor prevents charging of the uncoated face. They report stacks of several hundred 50–70 nm sections with typically <10 nm lateral jitter and registration good enough to skip landmark-based alignment. The method is positioned to supply the volumes needed for complete local-circuit reconstruction.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods demonstration, not a completed connectome. 50 nm is described as a practical thickness limit in their hands then; 20 nm isotropic is aspirational. Dose, heating at low kV, and BSE angular/contrast differences versus TEM are discussed as constraints. Oscillating-knife and ion-milling alternatives are prospective in the discussion.

ocar.opportunity: An essentially invariant, complete cellular anatomy would let connectivity of a whole nervous system be described neuron by neuron.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing that structure required serial electron micrographs through an entire small animal and consistent identification of processes, synapses, and neuromuscular junctions.
ocar.action: White, Southgate, Thomson, and Brenner reconstructed the hermaphrodite C. elegans nervous system from serial-section EM.
ocar.resolution: The hermaphrodite has 302 neurons in 118 morphological/connectivity classes. Neurons are simple, sparsely branched, and synapse en passant in stereotyped process bundles. Muscle arms reach motoneuron axons. A typical animal has about 5,000 chemical synapses, 2,000 neuromuscular junctions, and 600 gap junctions. Most morphologically identifiable connections are described, including amphids, nerve-ring and ventral-cord motoneurons, tail circuitry, and egg-laying.
ocar.future_work: Conclusions address process placement and synaptic specificity as organizing principles for this invariant nervous system.

summaries.beginner: This classic monograph maps every nerve cell in a tiny roundworm—302 of them—and lists how they connect with chemical synapses, muscle junctions, and electrical gap junctions. It is the original whole-animal wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (1986), White et al. deduce C. elegans hermaphrodite nervous-system structure from serial EM. They report 302 neurons, 118 classes, simple morphologies, en passant synapses in longitudinal and circumferential bundles, and muscle arms onto motoneuron axons. Typical synapse counts are about 5,000 chemical, 2,000 neuromuscular, and 600 gap junctions. Reliability, nomenclature, and circuit chapters (amphids, ventral cord, egg-laying) structure the 340-page account.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract is largely front matter and contents (pdf_chars_body is short relative to the 340-page work); counts in the abstract are the quantitative spine of this card. “Most” identifiable synapses in a typical animal are described, not a modern digital adjacency matrix. Structure is of the hermaphrodite; males differ. Later revisions of the worm connectome exist beyond this 1986 reconstruction.
